summary: Describes a way for a restarting IS-IS router to tell its neighbors it is restarting, so they can rebuild adjacencies without cycling through the down state while still synchronizing their databases. It also lets a router keep forwarding while it restarts. It was replaced by RFC 5306.

eli5.summary: If a bus driver takes a quick break, the other drivers are told so they do not think the driver is gone. This was replaced by RFC 5306.

questions: how does IS-IS handle router restart
subtitle: Minimize routing disruption when an IS-IS router restarts by using special signaling.

tldr.problem: When an IS-IS router restarts, neighbors detect the restart and cycle their adjacencies through the down state, causing widespread LSP regeneration and temporary routing disruption. Additionally, the restarting router computes routes before achieving database synchronization, creating non-convergent routing states.
tldr.mechanism: The restart mechanism introduces a new TLV in IIH packets with flags (RR, RA, SA) that allow a restarting router to signal its neighbors, who then maintain existing adjacencies without cycling through down state while still triggering database synchronization via CSNPs. Three timers (T1, T2, T3) coordinate the process and prevent premature SPF computation.
tldr.outcome: Routers can restart with minimal transient routing disruption. The mechanism handles both restarting routers (which maintain forwarding state) and starting routers (which do not), optimizing database synchronization in each case. RFC 5306 later refined these procedures.

facts.label: Restart TLV flags
facts.value: RR (Restart Request), RA (Restart Acknowledgement), SA (Suppress Adjacency Advertisement)

today: RFC 5306 supersedes this document with refined restart procedures and additional optimizations.

sections.title: Introduction to IS-IS Restart
sections.content:
IS-IS is a link-state routing protocol used to exchange routing information within a network domain. When an IS-IS router restarts—either due to control plane crash or maintenance—normally neighbors react by cycling their adjacencies through a down state. This triggers the neighbors to regenerate their LSPs (Link State Packets) describing the adjacency, causing SPF (Shortest Path First) computations throughout the domain and transient routing disruption.

This document introduces a mechanism for a restarting router to signal its restart to neighbors, allowing them to maintain adjacencies without state cycling while still correctly triggering database synchronization. The mechanism also applies to routers that are starting fresh (with no maintained forwarding state) and optimizes the synchronization process to minimize disruption.
sections.eli5: When a router wakes up after a crash, its neighbors normally think it is gone for good and update their maps. This RFC lets the router say "I am still here, just rebooting" so everyone stays calm while things get back in sync.

sections.title: The Restart Problem
sections.content:
When an IS-IS router is restarted, two sources of disruption occur. First, the restarting router computes its own routes before achieving database synchronization with its neighbors, resulting in non-convergent routing. Second, the restarting router's neighbors detect the restart event and cycle their adjacencies through the down state, regenerating their LSPs and causing SPF runs throughout the area or domain.

Each of these actions is necessary under normal operation. The neighbor's LSP regeneration sets SRMflags (Set Retransmit flags) to ensure the LSP database is synchronized, and the CSNP (Complete Sequence Number PDU) transmission provides a means of determining when synchronization is complete. However, when a router is merely restarting (not failing and being replaced), this disruption is highly undesirable and can cause transient blackholes or suboptimal routing.
sections.eli5: Two bad things happen: first, the restarting router sends out bad route information before it knows what is actually working, and second, its neighbors get confused and broadcast that the router is broken, making everyone recalculate their paths.

sections.title: Restart Signaling Mechanism
sections.content:
The solution introduces a new TLV (Type-Length-Value) field in IIH (IS-IS Hello) packets. This TLV carries three flag bits: RR (Restart Request), RA (Restart Acknowledgement), and SA (Suppress Adjacency Advertisement). A restarting router sets the RR bit to signal neighbors that restart is in progress. Neighbors respond with the RA bit set to acknowledge the restart and maintain the adjacency without state cycling.

When a neighbor receives an IIH with RR set for an adjacency already in the UP state, it performs three critical actions without cycling the adjacency: it marks the adjacency as being in "Restart mode", refreshes the holding time, and immediately transmits a complete set of CSNPs and sets SRMflags. This ensures the LSP database will be synchronized while avoiding the LSP regeneration that would normally occur.

The mechanism also defines three timers. Timer T1 (per interface) controls retransmission of restart requests. Timer T2 (per LSPDB) bounds the maximum time for synchronization. Timer T3 (system-wide) serves as a timeout for the restarting router to declare that database synchronization has not been achieved.
sections.eli5: A special label in hello messages says "I am restarting." Neighbors see this and agree to keep the connection open and send their database information, all without broadcasting the bad news to the whole network.

sections.title: Adjacency Handling for Restart and Start
sections.content:
A restarting router (one that maintains forwarding state across the restart) initializes three timers on restart: T1 for each interface, T2 for each LSPDB, and T3 system-wide. It then transmits IIHs with the RR bit set until it receives acknowledgement and a complete set of CSNPs over each interface. The router MUST NOT transmit its own LSPs or update forwarding tables while timer T3 is running.

A starting router (one that does not maintain forwarding state) uses a different approach. It sends IIHs with the SA bit set, asking neighbors to suppress advertisement of the adjacency in their LSPs until the starting router has propagated newer versions of its previously generated LSPs. The starting router sends its zeroth LSP immediately with the overload bit set, preventing other routers from computing paths through it until synchronization is complete. This avoids temporary blackholes that could occur if old LSPs from a previous incarnation appear newer than the new LSP versions the starting router generates.
sections.eli5: A restarting router (which kept forwarding working) uses RR to stay quiet while learning what changed. A new router uses SA to ask neighbors "do not tell anyone about me yet" while it figures out what LSPs it should have.

sections.title: Synchronizing the Link State Database
sections.content:
The first complete set of CSNPs received over each interface tells the restarting router which LSPs are currently held by each neighbor. The router records these LSPID entries along with their remaining lifetime. As normal LSP flooding proceeds, entries are removed when the corresponding LSP arrives or when the remaining lifetime expires. When the LSPID list is empty and timer T1 has been cancelled for all interfaces, timer T2 is cancelled, indicating database synchronization is complete.

For a restarting router, once all T2 timers have expired or been cancelled (meaning all LSP databases are synchronized), SPF is computed and forwarding tables are updated. If timer T3 expires before all T2 timers are cancelled (indicating synchronization is taking longer than the minimum holding time of neighbors), the router floods its LSP with the overload bit set to prevent routing through it, and resumes normal operation with eventual synchronization through standard LSP flooding. For a starting router, synchronization allows clearing the overload bit in the zeroth LSP and proceeding to normal operation.
sections.eli5: Neighbors send lists of what LSPs they have. The restarting router checks off items as it receives them. Once it has everything, it is safe to route traffic through it again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security properties of this mechanism depend on the ability of an attacker to inject false IS-IS PDUs, which has not been made easier by these procedures. If an attacker sets the RR bit in a false IIH, neighbors will maintain an adjacency that might otherwise expire and may unnecessarily send CSNPs. While wasteful, this causes no disruption to correct protocol operation. If the RA bit is set falsely, a restarting router may falsely believe a neighbor supports the restart procedures and wait longer for CSNPs before timing out. If the SA bit is set falsely, a neighbor may suppress adjacency advertisement indefinitely, potentially causing loss of reachability. The use of IS-IS authentication, especially cryptographic authentication, reduces the possibility of PDU spoofing.
sections.eli5: An attacker could pretend to be restarting and waste neighbor CPU time, or suppress the announcement of a connection. Regular IS-IS authentication prevents this.
